title: How long?
hook: the Psalms let the faithful complain: how long, O Lord? (Psalm 13)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the whirlwind: God answers Job with stars, sea and wild things, not a reason. Your line was where were you. Today, from Job to the Psalms.

"Are we there yet?" From the back seat, the first time, it's almost cute. By the fourth time, it's a different question. It isn't asking about the map anymore. It's saying: this is too long, I'm tired, and I don't know if it ends. Grown-ups ask it too, in hospital corridors, in long months out of work, at three in the morning. And the book of Psalms, a book of prayers, keeps that question right inside it.
screen: `ARE WE THERE YET?` → `BY THE FOURTH TIME, A DIFFERENT QUESTION.` → `THE PSALMS KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: First, four times. Psalm thirteen opens: "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?" The next verse keeps going: "How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?" How long, four times, in two verses: the back seat, at the fourth asking. Second, for ever? Tucked into the first line is the fear under the question. Not just how long, but: is this forever? Has God forgotten me for good? The psalm says that out loud, to God, in a prayer. Third, a complaint in the prayer book. This isn't a private diary that slipped in by mistake. The psalm sits in the book of prayers that Jews and Christians both pray, and its heading gives it to the chief musician, as a psalm of David. Complaint, here, is part of worship: a faithful voice asking God, are you hiding, and how long? Fourth, the turn. Near the end the psalm turns: "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation." And the last line: "I will sing unto the LORD, because he hath dealt bountifully with me." Look closely. The psalm never says the trouble ended. The enemy isn't said to have left; the sorrow isn't said to be gone. The turn to trust comes inside the waiting, not after it. Some readers hear that as the heart of the psalm: the how long and the but I have trusted, side by side, in one short prayer.
screen: `HOW LONG, FOUR TIMES.` · `FOR EVER?` · `A COMPLAINT IN THE PRAYER BOOK.` · `THE TURN COMES INSIDE THE WAITING.` · then, large: `HOW LONG.`

segments.voice: Find one thing in your life that's taking too long, a healing, an answer, a person coming round, and form your own how long: one honest sentence starting with those two words. Write it down if there's paper nearby, or word by word in your head, and read it back once. Then leave it on the page, unanswered, with no need for a happy ending.
How long?: the question Psalm thirteen asks four times, a faithful person's complaint kept right inside the book of prayers. Today's word.
Your line: but I have trusted. The trust comes inside the waiting, not after it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians pray the Psalms, alone and together; psalms of complaint like Psalm 13 are part of that prayer, and some people pray them in times of illness, grief or long waiting.

pairs: asked four times in two verses

fork.setup: you're praying Psalm 13. you've asked how long, four times, and nothing has changed yet. how does the psalm go on?
options: it waits until the enemy is gone, then gives thanks
it turns: but I have trusted in thy mercy

original.note: Hebrew: how long, the words that open Psalm 13.

trapdoor: what you thought: a person of faith isn't supposed to complain to God.
what it means: Psalm 13 asks how long, four times, and keeps the complaint inside a prayer.
what a scholar hears: the psalm moves from complaint (13:1–2) to request (13:3–4) to trust and song (13:5–6), a shape some readers call a psalm of lament.
recall: gave the Stoic school its logic
guess: the psalm's cry, asked four times, kept inside the prayer book
a prophet's question about the date the world will end
a prayer asking the length of a fast before a feast

chat.says: Does the trouble in Psalm thirteen get fixed before it turns to trust?
options: No; it turns to trust inside the waiting, before anything is said to change.
Yes; the enemy leaves first, and only then does the psalm give thanks.
No; the psalm ends still asking how long, with no turn to trust at all.
chat.meaning: The psalm never says the trouble ended. "But I have trusted in thy mercy" comes inside the waiting, beside the how long.

notes: Editor: 'the faithful are allowed to say: where are you' (a narrator ruling, and words not in the psalm) changed to what the psalm itself asks; stock 'here's what's worth noticing' cut; practice now writes the how long (as the index asks) instead of repeating the 'if you pray, say it to God; if not, say it to...' pattern used in days 711 and 714.
The count 'four times' is taken directly from the KJV text of 13:1–2 (How long ×2, how long ×2); confirm it holds in the Hebrew (עַד־אָנָה ×4).
The heading 'To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David' is paraphrased; in the Hebrew it is verse 1, so verse numbers differ between Hebrew and English Bibles.
Original: עַד־אָנָה with pronunciation ahd-ah-NAH; confirm.
